relationship: Judgment imagery: the wicked person's support shattered
rationale: Ezekiel says that the lawless person's support will be shattered in the approaching judgment. The psalm contrasts the shattered arms of sinners with the Lord sustaining the righteous. Both portray the failure of what sustains the wicked through shattering imagery. The psalm names arms, whereas Ezekiel says support, and it does not explain Ezekiel's qualification about neither tumult nor haste.
source_text: It will shatter the support of a lawless person, neither with tumult nor with haste.

target_units.text: For the arms of sinners will be shattered, but the Lord sustains the righteous.

relationship: Animal imagery: foxes as a rebuke to hostile leaders
rationale: Ezekiel calls Israel's false prophets foxes in the wildernesses. When warned that Herod wants to kill Him, Jesus calls Herod that fox while continuing His work and journey. Both apply a fox designation negatively to influential human figures in a prophetic confrontation. Herod is not identified as one of Ezekiel's prophets, and neither passage requires an added explanation of a particular fox behavior.
source_text: Your prophets, Israel, are like foxes in the wildernesses.

target_units.text: At that very hour some Pharisees approached and said to Him, “Leave and go away from here, because Herod wants to kill Thee.”
And He said to them, “Go and tell that fox, ‘Behold, I drive out demons and accomplish healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am brought to completion.’
Nevertheless, I must travel today and tomorrow and the day following, because it is not possible for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem.

relationship: Narrative contrast: newborn care withheld and supplied
rationale: Ezekiel's personified Jerusalem lacks several forms of newborn care, explicitly including swaddling cloths. Luke describes Mary giving birth and wrapping her firstborn Son in swaddling cloths even though lodging space was unavailable. The correspondence contrasts the absence and provision of that specific infant care. Luke does not supply Ezekiel's washing, salting or breast-binding actions, and Jerusalem's allegorical birth is not treated as Jesus' birth.
source_text: As for your birth, on the day you were born they did not bind your breasts; you were not washed with water, not salted with salt, and not wrapped in swaddling cloths.

target_units.text: While they were there, the time came for her to give birth.
She bore her firstborn Son, wrapped Him in swaddling cloths, and laid Him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the lodging place.

relationship: Narrative contrast: an exposed infant and compassion
rationale: Ezekiel describes Jerusalem cast onto the plain on the day of birth and explicitly says My eye did not spare her or feel for her. Exodus describes an infant placed in a basket by the river and Pharaoh's daughter seeing him weep and having compassion. Both scenes focus on a vulnerable exposed infant and the response of the one who sees, but the expressed responses contrast. Exodus does not attribute crookedness to the child, and Ezekiel's My eye is not changed into an unnamed passerby's eye.
source_text: Nor did My eye spare you to do any of all these things for you, to feel anything for you. You were cast upon the face of the plain because of your life’s crookedness, on the day you were born.

target_units.text: When they could no longer hide him, his mother took a basket for him and coated it with bitumen-pitch. She put the child in it and placed it in the marsh beside the river.
His sister watched from a distance to learn what would happen to him.
Pharaoh’s daughter came down to bathe at the river while her attendants walked beside it. She saw the basket in the marsh, sent her attendant, and had it brought to her.
And she opened it, and saw a child weeping in the basket; and Pharaoh’s daughter had compassion on him, and said, “This is one of the Hebrew children.”

relationship: Theological contrast: commands, goodness and life
rationale: Ezekiel reports God giving commands that were not good and ordinances in which the people would not live. Paul describes the commandment intended for life proving to bring death, yet insists that the commandment itself is holy, righteous and good, with sin causing the death. Both explicitly discuss commands in relation to life and death, but their claims about goodness differ. The comparison preserves that difference and does not identify Ezekiel's commands with Paul's commandment or explain away Ezekiel's divine agency.
source_text: I too gave them commands that were not good, and ordinances in which they would not live.

target_units.text: and I died; and the commandment that was for life proved to bring me death.
For sin, taking opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.
So the law is holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good.

Did the good, then, become death to me? May it never be! But sin did, so that it might appear as sin, producing death in me through the good, so that through the commandment sin might become sinful beyond measure.

relationship: Within-book imagery: disabling a nation's bodily strength
rationale: God announces the paralysis of Moab's shoulder in the judgment on its frontier territory. The Egypt oracle depicts Pharaoh's shattered arms unable to hold a sword, contrasting them with the strengthened arms of Babylon's king. Both national-judgment oracles use a disabled upper limb to portray power being overcome. Moab's shoulder is not changed into Pharaoh's arms, and this comparison does not resolve Asimouth or the source's geographical details.
source_text: therefore behold, I am paralyzing Moab’s shoulder from its frontier cities, the choice land, the house of Asimouth above a spring of a coastal city.

target_units.text: “Son of man, I shattered the arms of Pharaoh king of Egypt. Behold, it has not been bound up to provide healing, to put a poultice upon it, to give strength to grasp a sword.
Therefore thus says the Lord, the Lord: Behold, I am against Pharaoh king of Egypt. I will shatter his arms, the strong and the outstretched, and cast his sword down from his hand,
and scatter Egypt into the nations and winnow them into the countries.
I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon and put My sword into his hand; he will bring it upon Egypt, take her booty, and strip her spoils.

I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, but Pharaoh’s arms will fall. They will know that I am the Lord when I put My sword into the hands of the king of Babylon and he stretches it over the land of Egypt.

relationship: Underworld imagery: fallen powers among giants in Hades
rationale: Ezekiel places the fallen with ancient giants who descended to Hades carrying weapons. Isaiah's lament over Babylon's king portrays the giants who ruled the earth rising in Hades and acknowledging that the arriving king has been numbered with them. Both bring fallen earthly power into the company of giants in Hades. Isaiah does not describe swords beneath heads or deeds upon bones, and no particular giant or king is equated between the scenes.
source_text: They lay with the giants who fell long ago, who descended to Hades with weapons of war and put their swords beneath their heads. Their lawless deeds were upon their bones, because they terrified giants in the land of life.

target_units.text: Hades below grew bitter on meeting you. All the giants who ruled the earth rose together for you, those who raised all the nations’ kings from their thrones.
They will all answer and say to you, ‘You too were captured as we were, and were numbered among us.’
Your glory went down to Hades, your abundant gladness. They will spread decay beneath you, and your covering is a worm.

relationship: Judgment contrast: earth's rejoicing alongside an enemy's fall
rationale: Ezekiel sets the whole earth's rejoicing beside God's making Mount Seir a wilderness. Isaiah's lament against Babylon's king says the whole earth cries with gladness and the trees rejoice because their cutter no longer comes. Both set widespread rejoicing against the fall of a hostile power. The rejoicing earth is the shared subject; Seir's desolation is not equated with Babylon's king or with Idumea rejoicing over Judah.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: In the rejoicing of the whole earth, I will make you a wilderness.

target_units.text: he rested confidently. The whole earth cries out with gladness,
and Lebanon’s trees rejoiced over you, and Lebanon’s cedar: ‘Since you have fallen asleep, the one cutting us has not come up.’
